..
Issued at 156 AM EST Thu Nov 12 2026

Today-Tonight...A substantial mid-upper level trough digs down 
the Central and Eastern US, developing a surface low centered over
the Ohio Valley that will slide east towards the Mid-Atlantic. An
initial weak front associated with this system has already moved 
into East Central Florida, bringing slightly lower temperatures 
while starting to usher moisture away, but we'll have to wait for 
a reinforcing front tomorrow before the colder and drier weather 
arrives. Lows this morning dip to the U50s-U60s. Afternoon highs 
will be a few degrees lower than yesterday in the U70s-L80s 
between the slightly cooler air and cloud cover. Westerly winds 
around 10 mph with gusts to around 20 mph. Isolated to widely 
scattered showers (chances 20-30%) and isolated lightning storms 
(chances 20% or less) will be possible from late morning into the 
afternoon from the Treasure Coast to Okeechobee where the higher 
moisture lingers in proximity to the front. Middling instability 
and fairly moist mid-levels aren't particularly favorable for 
strong storms, but mid-level temperatures are still cool, and 
can't rule out gusts to 40 mph and occasional lightning. To the 
north, there is a very low (less than 20%) chance for transient 
elevated showers. 

Friday-Saturday...The upper-level trough strengthens over the
eastern half of the CONUS, developing a broad mid-level low 
extending from the Great Lakes east to New England and down into 
the Deep South. While the mid-upper level system is forecast to 
stall for a few days, the deepening attendant surface low off the 
New England coast is expected to pivot northeast as a second 
stronger cold front bringing drier and cooler continental air 
pushes into Florida early Friday, finally delivering actually cool
temperatures. Lows Friday morning only dip a little to the 
M50s-U60s, but highs will be held to the 70s. Saturday morning 
will be properly chilly, though there is a little uncertainty just
how cold it will get inland/north. Clearing skies and radiational
cooling is likely to be offset by mixing from 5-10 mph winds 
continuing into the overnight, but those NW-NNW winds will also
keep advecting cooler air to Central Florida. In addition, if the
boundary layer decouples and winds go light, radiational cooling 
will be enhanced and could cause temperatures to quickly drop. NBM
has a 6 or so degree spread between the 75th-25th percentiles, 
and MOS guidance is close the 10th percentile. The official 
forecast generally falls a degree or two below NBM mean, calling 
for low temperatures in the M40s-L50s, lowest north of I-4, and 
mildest along the Space and Treasure Coasts. Those 5-10 mph winds 
will result in chills in the L-M40s for all but the Treasure 
Coast, and there is a very low chance to briefly dip to the U30s 
north of I-4. Daytime temperatures held to the 60s Saturday. Can't
rule out a few light showers down south on Friday, but otherwise 
dry conditions.

Sunday-Wednesday...The upper level pattern starts sliding east
again, pushing the mid-level low offshore and bringing a sharp
ridge from the Intermountain west over the eastern US, ushering 
the surface high to the Atlantic seaboard. Locally, winds shift 
back onshore (northeasterly to easterly), putting and end to the 
briefly chilly weather, gradually warming temperatures back to 
normal, and bringing back rain chances. Beyond that, confidence in
the forecast and potential impacts decreases considerably. There 
is good agreement a lobe or two of vorticity from the western US 
will undercut the ridge, sliding towards the Southeast and Gulf, 
but models remain inconsistent with timing and location. Agreement
on what happens at the surface is even worse. The GFS had been 
aggressively developing a surface low in the Gulf on the residual 
frontal boundary, then tracking the feature toward Florida. This 
scenario causes moisture to again surge across the area, bringing 
back the threat for locally heavy rainfall, and potentially 
dangerous beach and marine conditions. However, the ECM barely 
develops a surface wave while keeping the highest moisture 
generally south of the area, and the CMC falls in between these 
two solutions, developing a weaker low but still delivering above 
normal moisture a day or two later than the GFS timeline. The 
respective ensemble suites all reflect the deterministic guidance,
so no help there, and the 00Z GFS came in with significantly 
weaker mid-level energy and subsequently less development of the 
surface low, only adding to the forecast uncertainty. Will need to
monitor the threat for locally heavy rainfall Monday into mid- 
week, due to lingering effects of last week's extreme rainfall, 
but it is too early to determine if, when, or where heavy rainfall
may occur.
